sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go modules are how every Go project manages dependencies, and the toolchain (go command) is how you build, test, and generate code. Interviewers ask about modules to check that you understand the security model (go.sum checksums, GOPROXY), can diagnose dependency conflicts, and know when to use advanced features like workspaces and replace directives in a multi-module monorepo.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: go.mod defines what your module is and what it directly requires. go.sum locks the cryptographic checksums of all modules (direct and indirect) so builds are reproducible. The go command fetches modules via GOPROXY (default: proxy.golang.org) and verifies checksums against GONOSUMCHECK/GOSUM. Think of GOPROXY as npm registry and go.sum as a lockfile. A go workspace (go.work) lets multiple local modules reference each other without publishing—essential for monorepo development.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. go.mod: module path, go directive (minimum Go version), require blocks (direct and indirect), toolchain directive (Go 1.21+). 2. go.sum: hash of module zip + go.mod; never edit manually; checked on every build. 3. go get / go mod tidy: go get updates specific dep; tidy removes unused and adds missing indirect deps—run before every commit. 4. go workspace (go.work): go work init, go work use ./service-a ./service-b; replaces local replace directives for dev. 5. replace directive: redirect a module import to a local path or fork; use sparingly, document why. 6. vendoring: go mod vendor copies deps to /vendor; go build -mod=vendor uses it; useful for air-gapped builds. 7. go generate: //go:generate comment + go generate ./...; used for mockgen, protoc, stringer, sqlc. 8. Semantic versioning: v2+ modules must have /v2 in module path; major version incompatibility.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'What is the difference between go.mod and go.sum?' → go.mod declares requirements; go.sum locks checksums for reproducibility and supply-chain security. • 'How do you use a local fork of a dependency?' → replace directive in go.mod pointing to local path, or go workspace for multi-module repos. • 'When would you vendor dependencies?' → air-gapped CI environments, regulatory requirements for auditable source, guaranteed reproducibility without GOPROXY. • 'How does go mod tidy work and when do you run it?' → adds missing indirect deps, removes unused ones; run after any dependency change and in CI to detect drift.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "I treat go.mod and go.sum as part of the codebase—both are committed and reviewed. Before any PR I run go mod tidy and go mod verify to make sure the dependency tree is clean. In a monorepo with multiple Go modules I use go workspaces: go work init lists each module directory, so local changes in a shared library are immediately visible to all consuming services without publishing. If I need to patch a third-party library I prefer a replace directive with a clear comment explaining why and a tracking issue URL. For CI environments that can't reach the internet I vendor with go mod vendor and set GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor. I avoid manual edits to go.sum—if it diverges I run tidy and verify to fix it rather than force-editing.
